claims.text: The WHO 2024 guidance does not include evidence‑based criteria for stopping antibiotics at 36 hours after a negative culture in early‑onset neonatal sepsis.
Continue close clinical monitoring (temperature, respiratory rate, feeding tolerance, and activity) while awaiting further culture results or clinical improvement.
Escalate care if any new or worsening signs appear (e.g., fever >38.5 °C, respiratory distress, poor perfusion, or lethargy) despite ongoing antibiotics.
Maintain empiric antibiotic therapy beyond 36 hours in the absence of a validated stopping rule, given the lack of WHO guidance for early discontinuation.
Consider adjunctive biomarkers (CRP, procalcitonin) to aid decision‑making, recognizing moderate diagnostic performance reported by WHO systematic reviews.
Inform caregivers that antibiotic duration will be guided by clinical response and evolving evidence, not solely by a 36‑hour culture result.

packet.guideline: WHO serious bacterial infections 2024 (EOS subset), EVALUATION ONLY

patient.clinical_condition: hospitalized with suspected sepsis and persistent signs

packet.evaluation_question: Hospitalized suspected sepsis: a culture is negative at 36 hours but clinical signs persist. Does this WHO source provide a NICE-style 36-hour stopping pathway? Gestation 35 weeks; age 63 hours; setting hospital.

evidence.text: 0–6 days: Good sensitivity and fair specificity ᵃ of the 7-sign IMCI algorithm compared with physician judgement of sepsis as the reference standard; there was no evidence for either culture- confirmed sepsis or mortality as the reference standard.

0–59 days and 7–59 days: Fair sensitivity and fair specificity ᵃ of the 7-sign IMCI algorithm compared with physician judgement of sepsis as the reference standard; there was no evidence for either culture-confirmed sepsis or mortality as the reference standard.

Two additional systematic reviews examined the diagnostic accuracy of laboratory biomarkers to diagnose culture-confirmed sepsis (88) or clinical or culture-confirmed sepsis (89) in infants aged 0–59 days at the time of presentation to health facilities. Brown et al. (2019) identified 20 studies of 1615 infants reporting upon diagnostic accuracy of CRP in neonates and reported that at median specificity (0.74), sensitivity was 0.62 (95% CI: 0.50 to 0.73) (88). Rees et al. (2023) examined CRP, procalcitonin (PCT), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and white cell count (WCC) in 134 studies, and concluded that CRP and PCT demonstrated good discriminatory ability to diagnose sepsis with blood culture as the reference

Question: Among young infants aged 0–59 days with PSBI, in non-hospital settings, what is the diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity and specificity) of clinical sign-based algorithms of PSBIᵃ compared with a reference standard (culture-confirmed sepsis, physician judgement of sepsis, or mortality) in identifying infants who require treatment for PSBI?
